passage: I'm Dilnaz, and I sat next to Zeenat at Friday's town hall. The new director clicked through slides about 'rightsizing for agility' and 'releasing talent to the market'. People nodded. Zeenat raised her hand. 'Sorry, I just want to understand. Rightsizing means how many people lose their jobs, and in which teams?' The room went quiet. The director said, 'We're optimising roles.' Zeenat said, calmly, 'So, people. How many, and when will they be told?' After a long pause he said, 'About forty, mostly in support. Next month.' I saw the support team's faces at the back. Afterwards three of them came up and thanked her. I don't know what she felt, standing up like that. Her voice didn't shake. But when she sat down, her hand held the edge of her chair very tightly.

qa.q: How many people did the director say would be affected?
qa.a: The director said about forty, mostly in support.

qa.q: What might Zeenat's tight grip on the chair suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was nervous about speaking up even though her voice stayed calm; she cared enough about the people affected to do it anyway.

qa.q: Why was Zeenat's question so effective?
qa.a: Asking how many people, which teams and when turned soft words like 'rightsizing' into plain facts about real people, which the room could no longer look past.

qa.q: How might the support team at the back have felt after the question?
qa.a: The support team probably felt shaken but respected, since they finally heard what 'rightsizing' meant for them, which is why three came to thank Zeenat.

grounding: Shows, through a colleague's eyes, an adult who hears a layoff called rightsizing and asks plainly what happens to whom.

passage: Mehak, when the HR note said 'transition support for impacted resources', you frowned, and I liked that. Let me tell you why. Twenty years ago, at the textile mill office, I sat in a meeting where the owner's son called closing the dyeing unit 'streamlining'. Everyone clapped politely. I, Disha, was twenty-five and scared, but I asked, 'Streamlining means Mohan-bhai, Salim, the twelve dyers. What happens to them?' He didn't like it. But the word stopped working. Once we said their names, the meeting had to talk about notice, about wages, about moving some to the new unit. Eight of the twelve kept jobs. So when you see 'impacted resources', ask which people. Say their names out loud. It's the smallest thing you can do, and sometimes it's enough.

qa.q: How many of the twelve dyers kept jobs?
qa.a: Eight of the twelve kept jobs.

qa.q: How did Disha feel before asking the question in the meeting?
qa.a: Disha was scared, twenty-five and in a room full of polite clapping, but cared more about the dyers than about fitting in.

qa.q: What made naming 'Mohan-bhai, Salim, the twelve dyers' powerful?
qa.a: Saying their names turned 'streamlining' into real people losing work, so the meeting had to discuss notice, wages and moves instead of hiding behind a soft word.

qa.q: How might the dyers have fared if nobody had asked?
qa.a: They might have learned of the closure with no notice or plan, their lives hidden behind 'streamlining'; being named gave eight of them a way to stay.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague recalling how asking which people a 'streamlining' would affect brought moral attention back and saved jobs.

passage:
Pallavi joined the quarterly call from a crowded local train, one bar of signal, eleven minutes before her stop. Uday, the operations head, was sharing a slide: 'Rightsizing the Nashik warehouse to optimise headcount.'
The picture froze. By the time the audio came back, he was already on the next slide.
Pallavi unmuted, a vendor shouting 'chai, chai' behind her. 'Uday, sorry, before we move on. In plain words: how many people lose their jobs, and who tells them?'
A pause. 'Twenty-two loaders. HR will email them on Friday.'
The chat box, silent all call, filled up. 'Email?' 'Some of them don't check email.' 'Can they hear it in person?'
Uday rubbed his forehead. 'Fair. I'll go to Nashik on Thursday and talk to them with HR. Pallavi, send me the questions you'd want answered if it were you.'
Her station came. She typed the list standing by the door.

qa.q: How many loaders at the Nashik warehouse were losing their jobs?
qa.a: Twenty-two loaders, and HR planned to email them on Friday.

qa.q: What did Pallavi want the call to notice when she unmuted despite the noise?
qa.a: She wanted everyone to see the actual people behind 'rightsizing', worried that the slide would move on before anyone asked who was affected and how.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the call, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Pallavi's plain question was the turning point; once Uday said 'twenty-two loaders' and 'email', others spoke up, and Uday chose to go to Nashik and tell them face to face.

qa.q: How might the twenty-two loaders be affected by the way the call went?
qa.a: Instead of learning by an email some might not even check, they will hear it in person with HR there to answer questions; the loss still hurts, but they are treated as people.

grounding: An employee hears a layoff called rightsizing and asks plainly how many people lose jobs and who tells them, which turns the meeting's attention to them.

At six in the morning, the central kitchen in Kochi smelled of onions and steam. Simran, the new floor manager, pinned a chart by the walk-in fridge: 'Motivation Wall: slowest three packers of the day.'
'It's just to push everyone a little,' she said, smiling. 'Healthy pressure.'
Maria, who had packed lunches here for four years, dried her hands. 'Can I ask what it does, exactly? Whose names go up, and then what?'
Simran blinked. 'The bottom three. They stay back to clean.'
'So Latha, who's slow because of her wrist, and the two boys who joined last week. Every day. In front of the delivery riders.'
Simran looked at the chart for a long moment. Latha was already at the sink, head down.
'I didn't think of it as names,' Simran said quietly. She unpinned it. 'Let's rotate the cleaning instead. And tell me who needs help getting faster.'

qa.q: What did Simran call the chart she pinned by the walk-in fridge?
qa.a: She called it the 'Motivation Wall', for the slowest three packers of the day.

qa.q: Why did the chart seem reasonable to Simran at first?
qa.a: Simran thought of it as healthy pressure that would push everyone a little; the word 'motivation' kept the real people, like Latha and the new boys, out of her mind.

qa.q: Which question changed Simran's decision, and why did it work?
qa.a: Maria's plain question, 'Whose names go up, and then what?'; it made Simran picture Latha and the new boys shamed every day, so she unpinned the chart and rotated the cleaning.

qa.q: What would it be like for Latha if the chart had stayed up?
qa.a: Latha would likely see her name on the wall almost every day in front of the riders, singled out for a wrist she cannot help; the 'motivation' would feel like public shame.

grounding: A worker hears pressure called motivation and asks exactly whose names go up and what happens to them, which makes the manager see the people.

passage: At my first job, my manager Kiran had a word for everything. Staying till eleven was 'ownership'. Weekend calls were 'passion'. When Reshma cried in the washroom after a third late night, Kiran called it 'growth pains'. I went along with the words for months. Then one Friday Kiran announced, 'We're motivating the team with a stretch target: everyone stays till the release is done.' Something snapped into focus. I asked, 'What does that actually mean for people? How many hours, and who's covering Reshma's childcare?' The room went quiet. Kiran said, 'Eshaan, it's just a push.' I said, 'A push is fine. But if it means fourteen-hour days for two weeks, let's say that, and then decide if it's fair.' We ended up splitting the release into two phases. Reshma mouthed 'thank you' across the table. I realised how much the nice words had been doing our thinking for us.

qa.q: What did Kiran call staying till eleven?
qa.a: Kiran called it 'ownership'.

qa.q: Why did something 'snap into focus' for Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan felt uneasy and protective of teammates like Reshma, and the word 'motivating' finally seemed to be hiding exhausting, unfair hours.

qa.q: What did naming it plainly lead to?
qa.a: Saying 'fourteen-hour days for two weeks' let the team judge whether it was fair, and the release was split into two phases.

qa.q: How did Reshma experience Eshaan's question?
qa.a: Reshma seemed relieved and grateful, mouthing 'thank you', since Reshma's childcare had been ignored under the word 'push'.

grounding: An adult hears pressure called motivation and asks what it actually means for people, and the plain words change the plan.

Supervisor's note, regional office, Thursday.
In today's sales review, Yash presented his plan to 'motivate' field staff: a daily ranking of all thirty reps read aloud on the morning call, with the bottom five named. He called it healthy pressure. Aditi, who joined us eight months ago, asked to speak. She asked what would actually happen to the bottom five, day after day, in front of their peers. Yash said they'd work harder. Aditi said, calmly, 'Or they'll be embarrassed every morning, and some of our best people will leave. Can we call it public shaming and then decide if we want it?' The room went quiet. Several managers were nodding. We agreed to share rankings privately with each rep instead, with coaching for anyone struggling. I've asked Aditi to help draft the new approach, and I'll thank her in Monday's meeting.

qa.a: It suggests she felt concerned for the reps but steady, wanting the plan judged by what it does to people rather than by its label.

qa.q: What change came from naming it plainly?
qa.a: Calling it public shaming led the meeting to share rankings privately with each rep, with coaching for anyone struggling.

passage:
Tuesday, late.
The town hall was forty minutes long and nobody said the word people. Mridul, our department head, said “rightsizing” eleven times. I counted. “Optimising the support layer.” “Aligning capacity.”
Everyone clapped at the end. I clapped too, then felt a bit sick about it.
At the question slot I put my hand up. My voice shook. I asked, “Which teams, and what happens to them? Do the support staff in Nagpur lose their jobs, and when?”
It went very quiet. Mridul paused, then said, “Around sixty roles in Nagpur, over three months.”
Sixty roles. Sixty people, many of whom I've trained on video calls. Madhavi with the twins. The new joiner who asked me how to set up his leave.
Afterward, two colleagues messaged me: “thank you for asking that.” I'm still shaky. But now we are talking about people, not a layer. — Yogesh

qa.q: How many times did Mridul say “rightsizing”?
qa.a: Mridul said “rightsizing” eleven times during the town hall.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel after clapping at the end of the town hall?
qa.a: Yogesh felt uneasy and a bit sick, because the soft words had hidden what was happening to real colleagues.

qa.q: Which question made the difference, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking which teams and what happens to them; the plain question forced an answer in people and months instead of labels.

qa.q: What is it like for the two colleagues who messaged Yogesh?
qa.a: They seem relieved and grateful that someone asked out loud what they may have been afraid to ask themselves.

grounding: The diary shows an employee meeting the label rightsizing by asking what actually happens to whom, which brings attention back to people.

Pallavi, who kept the accounts, read it twice. The Pullur point was simply missing.

“I didn't think of it as people,” he said quietly. “Let's put it in the committee meeting on Friday. Write down those names for me.”

Subject: Question about "restructuring" in Tuesday's memo
Dear Keerthana,
Thank you for Tuesday's memo. I read it three times, and I'm still not sure what it means for my team.
The memo says the field support unit will be "restructured to improve efficiency" and that some roles will be "realigned". I understand the aim. But could you tell me plainly: will any of my eleven field staff lose their jobs, be moved to another city, or have their pay changed? If so, who, and from when?
I'm asking because the staff are already worried, and I would rather give them the truth than guess. Several of them have families in the district and no other work nearby.
If there are decisions still open, I'd also like to know how we can suggest options, such as reduced hours instead of cuts.
Thank you for your help.
Regards,
Manjula

qa.q: How many field staff does Manjula have?
qa.a: Manjula has eleven field staff.

qa.q: Why does Manjula ask for plain answers instead of accepting the memo's words?
qa.a: Manjula feels worried for the staff and uneasy that "realigned" hides real changes to people's jobs, pay and homes.

qa.q: What makes Manjula's email a good way to raise the concern?
qa.a: It is polite, asks exactly what happens to whom and when, and suggests alternatives like reduced hours.

qa.q: What might the field staff be feeling while waiting for an answer?
qa.a: They are probably anxious and unsure, worried about their jobs and their families in the district.

grounding: An adult asks plainly what a vague restructuring memo means for the field team, turning soft words back into questions about real people.
